clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant axonal CMT distinguished by disproportionately severe sensory loss with acral complications.
Ulceromutilating features dominate: painless foot ulcers, recurrent soft-tissue infection, osteomyelitis, Charcot joints and sometimes autoamputation of toes.
Marked phenotypic overlap with hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy, so some pedigrees are difficult to classify.
Nerve conduction shows an axonal pattern with reduced sensory and motor amplitudes and relatively preserved velocities.
Caused by RAB7A missense mutations affecting a small GTPase that controls late endosomal and lysosomal trafficking.
Distal weakness and pes cavus occur, but the sensory and trophic features usually overshadow the motor deficit.
Meticulous foot care and injury prevention are the cornerstone of management to avoid mutilating complications.
reference.pathophysiology: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2B is caused by heterozygous missense mutations in RAB7A, which encodes a ubiquitously expressed small GTPase that regulates transport between late endosomes and lysosomes and the trafficking and signalling of neurotrophin receptors such as the nerve growth factor receptor. Disease-causing substitutions cluster around the guanine nucleotide-binding region and behave as gain-of-function or dysregulated variants that perturb the cycling between GTP-bound and GDP-bound states. The resulting aberrant endosomal signalling is thought to particularly affect the longest, most metabolically demanding sensory axons, producing a length-dependent axonal degeneration with striking sensory predominance and the trophic, ulceromutilating complications that characterise the subtype.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy types I and II
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography confirming an axonal sensorimotor pattern
Hereditary neuropathy gene panel including RAB7A
Radiographs of feet for osteomyelitis and neuropathic (Charcot) joint changes
Structured skin and wound assessment of the feet
Screening to exclude acquired causes of a painless sensory neuropathy
Quantitative sensory testing to characterise the sensory deficit
redFlags: Painless deep ulcer with surrounding cellulitis or discharge suggesting osteomyelitis
Systemic features of sepsis arising from a foot infection
Rapidly progressive sensory loss pointing to an acquired cause
reference.prognosis: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2B is slowly progressive with generally normal life expectancy, but morbidity is driven by recurrent foot ulceration, infection and the risk of amputation from the mutilating acropathy.
pitfalls: Attributing foot ulcers purely to trauma or diabetes and missing the hereditary sensory neuropathy.
Providing inadequate protective footwear and foot surveillance, allowing preventable ulceration.
Classifying the disorder as a pure hereditary sensory neuropathy and overlooking coexisting motor involvement.
Delaying imaging for osteomyelitis because the ulcer is painless.
references: Charcot-Marie-Tooth hereditary neuropathy overview (clinical genetics reference)
Adams and Victor's principles of neurology
management: No disease-modifying drug therapy exists; care is supportive and rehabilitative through a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Meticulous protective foot care with regular podiatry, cushioned footwear and daily skin surveillance to pre-empt painless neuropathic ulceration
Prompt wound management with offloading, debridement and anti-staphylococcal antibiotics for infected ulcers and osteomyelitis
Orthopaedic management of neuropathic (Charcot) joints and acral deformity, with reconstructive surgery considered to avert autoamputation
Physiotherapy, stretching and ankle-foot orthoses for distal weakness and pes cavus
Neuropathic pain control with gabapentinoids or tricyclic agents
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine that can accelerate axonal loss
Autosomal dominant genetic counselling and screening of at-risk relatives
